{{Short description|Theorem representing a solvable Lie algebra}}
{{Distinguish|Lie's third theorem}}

In mathematics, specifically the theory of [[Lie algebra]]s, '''Lie's theorem''' states that,<ref name="Serre theorem">{{harvnb|Serre|2001|loc=Theorem 3}}</ref> over an [[algebraically closed field]] of characteristic zero, if <math>\pi: \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(V)</math> is a finite-dimensional [[representation of a Lie algebra|representation]] of a [[solvable Lie algebra]], then there is a [[flag (linear algebra)|flag]] <math>V = V_0 \supset V_1 \supset \cdots \supset V_n = 0</math> of [[invariant_subspace|invariant subspaces]] of <math>\pi(\mathfrak{g})</math> with <math>\operatorname{codim} V_i = i</math>,  meaning that <math>\pi(X)(V_i) \subseteq V_i</math> for each <math>X \in \mathfrak{g}</math> and ''i''.

Put in another way, the theorem says there is a basis for ''V'' such that all linear transformations in <math>\pi(\mathfrak{g})</math> are represented by upper triangular matrices.<ref>{{harvnb|Humphreys|1972|loc=Ch. II, § 4.1., Corollary A.}}</ref> This is a generalization of the result of Frobenius that [[commuting matrices]] are simultaneously [[Triangularizability|upper triangularizable]], as commuting matrices generate an [[abelian Lie algebra]], which is a fortiori solvable.

A consequence of Lie's theorem  is that any finite dimensional solvable Lie [[algebra over a field]] of characteristic 0 has a nilpotent [[derived algebra of a Lie algebra|derived algebra]] (see [[#Consequences]]). Also, to each flag in a finite-dimensional vector space ''V'', there correspond a [[Borel subalgebra]] (that consist of linear transformations stabilizing the flag); thus, the theorem says that <math>\pi(\mathfrak{g})</math> is contained in some Borel subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak{gl}(V)</math>.<ref name="Serre theorem" />

== Counter-example ==
For algebraically closed fields of characteristic ''p''>0 Lie's theorem holds provided the dimension of the representation is less than ''p'' (see the proof below), but can fail for representations of dimension ''p''. An example is given by the 3-dimensional nilpotent Lie algebra spanned by 1, ''x'', and ''d''/''dx'' acting on the ''p''-dimensional vector space ''k''[''x'']/(''x''<sup>''p''</sup>), which has no eigenvectors. Taking the [[semidirect product]] of this 3-dimensional Lie algebra by the ''p''-dimensional representation (considered as an abelian Lie algebra) gives a solvable Lie algebra whose derived algebra is not nilpotent.

== Proof ==
The proof is by induction on the dimension of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> and consists of several steps. (Note: the structure of the proof is very similar to that for [[Engel's theorem]].) The basic case is trivial and we assume the dimension of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is positive. We also assume ''V'' is not zero. For simplicity, we write <math>X \cdot v = \pi(X)(v)</math>.

'''Step 1''': Observe that the theorem is equivalent to the statement:<ref>{{harvnb|Serre|2001|loc=Theorem 3{{''}}}}</ref>
*There exists a vector in ''V'' that is an eigenvector for each linear transformation in <math>\pi(\mathfrak{g})</math>.
Indeed, the theorem says in particular that a nonzero vector spanning <math>V_{n-1}</math> is a common eigenvector for all the linear transformations in <math>\pi(\mathfrak{g})</math>. Conversely, if ''v'' is a common eigenvector, take <math>V_{n-1}</math> to be its span and then <math>\pi(\mathfrak{g})</math> admits a common eigenvector in the quotient <math>V/V_{n-1}</math>; repeat the argument.

'''Step 2''': Find an ideal <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> of codimension one in <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.

Let <math>D\mathfrak{g} = [\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{g}]</math> be the [[derived algebra of a Lie algebra|derived algebra]]. Since <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is solvable and has positive dimension, <math>D\mathfrak{g} \ne \mathfrak{g}</math> and so the quotient <math>\mathfrak{g}/D\mathfrak{g}</math> is a nonzero abelian Lie algebra, which certainly contains an ideal of codimension one and by the ideal correspondence, it corresponds to an ideal of codimension one in <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.

'''Step 3''': There exists some [[Linear form|linear functional]] <math>\lambda</math> in <math>\mathfrak{h}^*</math> such that
:<math>V_{\lambda} = \{ v \in V | X \cdot v = \lambda(X) v, X \in \mathfrak{h} \}</math>
is nonzero. This follows from the inductive hypothesis (it is easy to check that the eigenvalues determine a linear functional).

'''Step 4''': <math>V_{\lambda}</math> is a <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-invariant subspace. (Note this step proves a general fact and does not involve solvability.)

Let <math>Y \in \mathfrak{g}</math>, <math>v \in V_{\lambda}</math>, then we need to prove <math>Y \cdot v \in V_{\lambda}</math>. If <math>v = 0</math> then it's obvious, so assume <math>v \ne 0</math> and set recursively <math>v_0 = v, \, v_{i+1} = Y \cdot v_i</math>. Let <math>U = \operatorname{span} \{ v_i | i \ge 0 \}</math> and <math>\ell \in \mathbb{N}_0</math> be the largest such that <math>v_0,\ldots,v_\ell</math> are linearly independent. Then we'll prove that they generate ''U'' and thus <math>\alpha = (v_0,\ldots,v_\ell)</math> is a basis of ''U''. Indeed, assume by contradiction that it's not the case and let <math>m \in \mathbb{N}_0</math> be the smallest such that <math>v_m \notin \langle v_0,\ldots,v_\ell\rangle</math>, then obviously <math>m \ge \ell + 1</math>. Since <math>v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell+1}</math> are linearly dependent, <math>v_{\ell+1}</math> is a linear combination of <math>v_0,\ldots,v_\ell</math>. Applying the map <math>Y^{m-\ell-1}</math> it follows that <math>v_m</math> is a linear combination of <math>v_{m-\ell-1},\ldots,v_{m-1}</math>. Since by the minimality of ''m'' each of these vectors is a linear combination of <math>v_0,\ldots,v_\ell</math>, so is <math>v_m</math>, and we get the desired contradiction. We'll prove by induction that for every <math>n \in \mathbb{N}_0</math> and <math>X \in \mathfrak{h}</math> there exist elements <math>a_{0,n,X},\ldots,a_{n,n,X}</math> of the base field such that <math>a_{n,n,X}=\lambda(X)</math> and
:<math>X \cdot v_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n} a_{i,n,X}v_i.</math>
The <math>n=0</math> case is straightforward since <math>X \cdot v_0 = \lambda(X) v_0</math>. Now assume that we have proved the claim for some <math>n \in \mathbb{N}_0</math> and all elements of <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> and let <math>X \in \mathfrak{h}</math>. Since <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> is an ideal, it's <math>[X,Y] \in \mathfrak{h}</math>, and thus
:<math>X \cdot v_{n+1} = Y \cdot (X \cdot v_n) + [X, Y] \cdot v_n = Y \cdot \sum_{i=0}^{n} a_{i,n,X}v_i + \sum_{i=0}^{n} a_{i,n,[X,Y]}v_i = a_{0,n,[X,Y]}v_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} (a_{i-1,n,X} + a_{i,n,[X,Y]})v_i + \lambda(X)v_{n+1},</math>
and the induction step follows. This implies that for every <math>X \in \mathfrak{h}</math> the subspace ''U'' is an invariant subspace of ''X'' and the matrix of the restricted map <math>\pi(X)|_U</math> in the basis <math>\alpha</math> is upper triangular with diagonal elements equal to <math>\lambda(X)</math>, hence <math>\operatorname{tr}(\pi(X)|_U) = \dim(U) \lambda(X)</math>. Applying this with <math>[X,Y] \in \mathfrak{h}</math> instead of ''X'' gives <math>\operatorname{tr}(\pi([X,Y])|_U) = \dim(U) \lambda([X,Y])</math>. On the other hand, ''U'' is also obviously an invariant subspace of ''Y'', and so
:<math>\operatorname{tr}(\pi([X,Y])|_U) = \operatorname{tr}([\pi(X),\pi(Y)]|_U]) = \operatorname{tr}([\pi(X)|_U, \pi(Y)|_U]) = 0</math>
since commutators have zero trace, and thus <math>\dim(U) \lambda([X,Y]) = 0</math>. Since <math>\dim(U) > 0</math> is invertible (because of the assumption on the characteristic of the base field), <math>\lambda([X, Y]) = 0</math> and
:<math>X \cdot (Y \cdot v) = Y \cdot (X \cdot v) + [X, Y] \cdot v = Y \cdot (\lambda(X) v) + \lambda([X, Y]) v = \lambda(X) (Y \cdot v),</math>
and so <math>Y \cdot v \in V_{\lambda}</math>.

'''Step 5''': Finish up the proof by finding a common eigenvector.

Write <math>\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{h} + L</math> where ''L'' is a one-dimensional vector subspace. Since the base field is algebraically closed, there exists an eigenvector in <math>V_{\lambda}</math> for some (thus every) nonzero element of ''L''. Since that vector is also eigenvector for each element of <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>, the proof is complete. <math>\square</math>

== Consequences ==
The theorem applies in particular to the [[adjoint representation of a Lie algebra|adjoint representation]] <math>\operatorname{ad}: \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(\mathfrak{g})</math> of a (finite-dimensional) solvable Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero; thus, one can choose a basis on <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> with respect to which <math>\operatorname{ad}(\mathfrak{g})</math> consists of upper triangular matrices. It follows easily that for each <math>x, y \in \mathfrak{g}</math>, <math>\operatorname{ad}([x, y]) = [\operatorname{ad}(x), \operatorname{ad}(y)]</math> has diagonal consisting of zeros; i.e., <math>\operatorname{ad}([x, y])</math> is a strictly upper triangular matrix. This implies that <math>[\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g]</math> is a [[nilpotent Lie algebra]]. Moreover, if the base field is not algebraically closed then solvability and nilpotency of a Lie algebra is unaffected by extending the base field to its algebraic closure. Hence, one concludes the statement (the other implication is obvious):<ref>{{harvnb|Humphreys|1972|loc=Ch. II, § 4.1., Corollary C.}}</ref>
:''A finite-dimensional Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g</math> over a field of characteristic zero is solvable if and only if the derived algebra <math>D \mathfrak g = [\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g]</math> is nilpotent.''

Lie's theorem also establishes one direction in [[Cartan's criterion for solvability]]:
:''If ''V'' is a finite-dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic zero and <math>\mathfrak{g} \subseteq \mathfrak{gl}(V)</math> a Lie subalgebra, then <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is solvable if and only if <math>\operatorname{tr}(XY) = 0</math> for every <math>X \in \mathfrak{g}</math> and <math>Y \in [\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{g}]</math>.''<ref>{{harvnb|Serre|2001|loc=Theorem 4}}</ref>

Indeed, as above, after extending the base field, the implication <math>\Rightarrow</math> is seen easily. (The converse is more difficult to prove.)

Lie's theorem (for various ''V'') is equivalent to the statement:<ref>{{harvnb|Serre|2001|loc=Theorem 3'}}</ref>
:''For a solvable Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g</math> over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, each finite-dimensional simple <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-module (i.e., irreducible as a representation) has dimension one.''
Indeed, Lie's theorem clearly implies this statement. Conversely, assume the statement is true. Given a finite-dimensional <math>\mathfrak g</math>-module ''V'', let <math>V_1</math> be a maximal <math>\mathfrak g</math>-submodule (which exists by finiteness of the dimension). Then, by maximality, <math>V/V_1</math> is simple; thus, is one-dimensional. The induction now finishes the proof.

The statement says in particular that a finite-dimensional simple module over an [[abelian Lie algebra]] is one-dimensional; this fact remains true over any base field since in this case every vector subspace is a Lie subalgebra.<ref>{{harvnb|Jacobson|1979|loc=Ch. II, § 6, Lemma 5.}}</ref>

Here is another quite useful application:<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|Harris|1991|loc=Proposition 9.17.}}</ref>
:''Let <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero with [[radical of a Lie algebra|radical]] <math>\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak{g})</math>. Then each finite-dimensional simple representation <math>\pi: \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(V)</math> is the [[tensor product of representations|tensor product]] of a simple representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}/\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak{g})</math> with a one-dimensional representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> (i.e., a linear functional vanishing on Lie brackets).''

By Lie's theorem, we can find a linear functional <math>\lambda</math> of <math>\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak{g})</math> so that there is the weight space <math>V_{\lambda}</math> of <math>\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak{g})</math>. By Step 4 of the proof of Lie's theorem, <math>V_{\lambda}</math> is also a <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-module; so <math>V = V_{\lambda}</math>. In particular, for each <math>X \in \operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak{g})</math>, <math>\operatorname{tr}(\pi(X)) = \dim(V) \lambda(X)</math>. Extend <math>\lambda</math> to a linear functional on <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> that vanishes on <math>[\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g]</math>; <math>\lambda</math> is then a one-dimensional representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. Now, <math>(\pi, V) \simeq (\pi, V) \otimes (-\lambda) \otimes \lambda</math>. Since <math>\pi</math> coincides with <math>\lambda</math> on <math>\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak{g})</math>, we have that <math>V \otimes (-\lambda)</math> is trivial on <math>\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak{g})</math> and thus is the restriction of a (simple) representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}/\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak{g})</math>. <math>\square</math>
